HbA1c Test: Purpose, Procedure, Normal Range & Results
May 26, 2026 - By Lupin Diagnostics
India has over 10.1 crore people living with diabetes. A daily finger-prick reading captures just one moment. The HbA1c test normal range tells a fuller story. This simple blood test reveals your average blood sugar over three months. Here is everything you need to know about it.
What Is the HbA1c Test and How Does It Work?
Glucose in your blood naturally sticks to haemoglobin, the protein inside red blood cells. The more sugar in your blood, the more gets attached. Since red blood cells live for roughly three months, the HbA1c test captures your average blood sugar level over that entire period.
This makes it far more reliable than a single fasting reading. A fasting test changes with your last meal or stress levels. Glycated haemoglobin, on the other hand, reflects steady patterns. Think of it as a three-month report card for your blood sugar.
Here is how it differs from routine glucose checks:
A fasting blood sugar test measures glucose at one point in time.
The HbA1c test shows a percentage reflecting 90-day glucose control.
It does not swing based on a recent meal or exercise session.

I have voluntarily donated blood in this blood bank couple of times , however last afternoon I got a call from them stating that they have an emergency blood requirement, and if I can donate blood , I agreed, they said that I can either go by 4:00pm or tomorrow morning by 9am, since it was already 3:30 when they called and i wouldn't be able to reach in time I decided to go next morning 9am . When I reached no staff was there at the reception the two sisters were inside the ward which was a restricted area and were listening to music. I called them out loud but they didn't listen as they were engrossed in their music, i thought to call the landline, they completely ignored the landline, after waiting for 15 mins both the sisters came out. I told them I had got a call that there's an emergency hence have come for voluntary blood donation. However I was menstruating so will it be ok i donate blood. They told me they weren't aware so to wait for doctors who come at 9:30. I again waited till the doctor's arrived. None of the doctors cared to call me inside even knowing that I was waiting. After a while I asked the nurse if I could now go inside. There were 2 docs, one male n one female. The female doctor was applying make up and told me to wait for 5 more mins, and the male doctor was literally just sitting on his chair and doing nothing. I waited more it was almost 9:40 now , still they didn't have a little courtesy to call me inside. Again I went and told them sir ma'am I also have to reach to my workplace can you please now check , i asked them if I can donate blood when I was menstruating, and he just said a no. I got really annoyed and just asked him while I was waiting here for 50 mins couldn't you'll just inform me this. And why are sisters handling blood bank not aware about this basic thing? And he answered I am the doctor I know more.

After this whole incident I just had few questions.
1. Where was the emergency here? Staff including the doctors were taking their own sweet time to attend the donor

featured_reviews.name: Siddhesh Aparaj
featured_reviews.review_text:
My father was admitted this month under CGHS benefits for diabetic foot surgery. As very few hospitals in Mumbai are empanelled under Central Government Health Schemes, we were relieved to get admission here.

The OPD procedures went smoothly. We were later informed that the patient would need to be admitted for a short duration (around two days) for surgical treatment. Since a private room was unavailable at the time, we opted for a multi-sharing ward.

Overall, the surgical treatment and interactions with the doctors and specialists were excellent. Dr. Rajeev Singh and his team took great care of the patient and kept us informed about the surgery schedule in advance, ensuring the admission was not done unnecessarily early.

However, the experience with the nursing staff was disappointing. Routine procedures were frequently delayed, and when assistance was requested, the behaviour was often rude towards both patients and visitors. In contrast, the ward-boy staff were more cooperative, welcoming, and helpful.

The discharge process was particularly frustrating. It began around 10:30 AM, but the paperwork was not handled in a timely manner and took over six hours to complete. There was no clear communication, and responsibility for delays was repeatedly shifted between departments. Since both of my parents and many other patients in the ward are diabetic, such prolonged delays are especially challenging. This is not an overreaction, but a genuine concern.

Additionally, the behaviour at the cashier counter was unprofessional. The staff member was rude, provided no estimate of waiting time, did not manage the queue properly, and even threatened to call security when questioned politely.

I understand that healthcare jobs demand immense patience and resilience, but this also comes with a responsibility to maintain professionalism and empathy, especially towards patients who are already vulnerable.

I am unsure whether these issues stem from hospital management or understaffing, but there is clearly room for improvement and accountability.

Despite these concerns, I remain grateful for the medical care and treatment provided by the doctors and the hospital overall.
